Maonites
MAY-on-ites
n. pl.
Hebrew Maon, a habitation or dwelling; the Maonites are an Arabian people of the south, almost certainly the Mehunims of Chronicles. The same Hebrew word is used of God Himself as the dwelling place of His people, which gives the name an ironic edge.

Biblical Definition

The Maonites appear once by that name, in the LORD’s own recital of Israel’s deliverances when she came again to Him in the days of Jephthah: The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you; and ye cried to me, and I delivered you out of their hand (Judges 10:12). They are almost certainly the Mehunims whom Uzziah subdued — God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims (2 Chronicles 26:7) — and whom the Ammonites brought against Jehoshaphat. Their importance lies entirely in the sentence they stand in. Judges 10 is the LORD’s answer to a people who had served Baalim and Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Zidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines, and who now cried for deliverance. He lists seven oppressors He had already saved them from, and then says, Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation. The Maonites are one item in a divine indictment. And when Israel put away the strange gods and served the LORD, the record adds that his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. That is the God the Maonites were used to discipline, and the God who could not finally be provoked out of pity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no MAONITE entry. The Hebrew maon means a dwelling or habitation, and is the word used in Psalm 90:1 and Deuteronomy 33:27 for God as the refuge of His people.

MAONITES, n. pl. — An Arabian people south of Judah who oppressed Israel in the days of the judges; probably the Mehunims of 2 Chronicles.

The Hebrew root maon signifies a dwelling, a habitation, a den.

The same word describes God in Psalm 90:1, Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.

2 Chronicles 20:1 and 26:7 mention the Mehunims among the confederacies against Judah, and the identification with the Maonites is the usual one.

There is also a Maon in the hill country of Judah, David’s hiding place and Nabal’s district (1 Samuel 23:24-25; 25:2), a distinct place of the same name.

Key Scripture

Judges 10:12 — "The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you; and ye cried to me, and I delivered you out of their hand."

2 Chronicles 26:7 — "And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims."

Judges 10:14 — "Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your tribulation."

Judges 10:16 — "And they put away the strange gods from among them, and served the LORD: and his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel."

Psalm 90:1 — "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations."

Modern Corruption

Judges 10:14 is one of the sharpest sentences God ever spoke to His own people, and it is almost never preached. A God who cannot say go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen is not the God of Scripture.

expand to see more

The therapeutic account of God cannot accommodate Judges 10:14. Israel cries in distress and God tells her to take the complaint to the gods she preferred. That is holy irony, and it is meant to wound. It is also the necessary preface to what follows: only after that word do they put away the strange gods, and only then does the text say that his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel. Repentance in Scripture is not produced by reassurance. It is produced by God refusing to be one option among the gods a man has chosen, and the refusal is itself an act of mercy. Any preaching that skips verse 14 to reach verse 16 has removed the instrument God used.

The second thing to notice is the impassibility question the King James phrase raises. His soul was grieved is an anthropopathism — Scripture’s way of speaking of God after the manner of men, so that creatures can understand what is unchangeably true of Him. The Reformed confession holds God to be without body, parts, or passions, and holds at the same time that the compassion here declared is real and not a fiction. God is not moved from outside as we are moved; His mercy is His own eternal nature turned toward His people in time. Open theism reads such verses as evidence that God changes His mind and learns; the classical doctrine reads them as God stooping to speak in our language about what He has always been.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Meunim or Maon (H4584), from maon (H4583), a dwelling or habitation; the same noun is used of God as His people’s dwelling place.

expand to see more

Hebrew maon (H4583) — a dwelling, habitation, den; Psalm 90:1 of God Himself.

Hebrew Meunim (H4586) — Mehunims; the people of 2 Chronicles 26:7 generally identified with the Maonites.

Hebrew lachats (H3905) — to press, to oppress; the verb of Judges 10:12.

Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short, to be shortened; the idiom behind his soul was grieved (Judges 10:16) is that God’s soul was shortened for Israel’s misery.

The Maon of 1 Samuel 23-25, in the hill country of Judah, is a separate location bearing the same common noun.

Usage

"The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you (Judges 10:12) — one name in a list of seven deliverances."

"Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen (Judges 10:14) — the sentence that produced Israel’s repentance."

"Against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims (2 Chronicles 26:7) — the same people under the Chronicler’s name."
